lessons.title: Mill Production Planning and Scheduling
lessons.body: Production planning starts with knowing your mill's capacity. A small roller mill in Kenya might process 500 kg of wheat per hour. If you run one 8-hour shift, that's 4,000 kg per day. But you need to schedule cleaning, maintenance, and breaks. Plan for 7 hours of actual milling per shift. That gives 3,500 kg daily. If you sell 50 kg bags of flour, that's 70 bags per day. Your weekly plan should match orders. For example, if a bakery needs 200 bags per week, you need 3 days of milling. Use a simple wall chart or a notebook to write down orders, wheat stock, and milling days. Many African millers use a 'first in, first out' rule for wheat. Schedule harder wheat first because it takes more power. Also, group similar flour types to reduce changeover time. Changeover from white flour to whole wheat takes about 30 minutes for cleaning. So, if you have multiple orders, mill all white flour first, then whole wheat. Power availability is a big issue. In Nigeria, many millers run generators during grid outages. Schedule milling during times when electricity is stable, often early morning. Keep a generator on standby but only run it when needed to save fuel. Labor: assign one person to feed wheat, one to monitor the mill, and one to bag flour. Train them to watch for jams. A jam can stop production for 20 minutes. So, preventive checks every hour. Finally, keep a daily log: wheat used, flour produced, downtime reasons. This helps you improve next week. For example, if you see frequent jams on Mondays, maybe the wheat is too wet from weekend rain. Adjust by drying wheat first.

lessons.title: Inventory Management for Wheat and Flour
lessons.body: Inventory management is about having enough wheat and flour without wasting money. Start by calculating your usage. If you mill 3,500 kg of wheat per day, you need 17,500 kg per week (5 days). But wheat prices fluctuate. In Tanzania, wheat prices are lower after harvest in August. So, buy in bulk then. But you need storage. A 20-tonne warehouse can hold about 400 bags of 50 kg. Ensure the floor is raised on pallets to prevent moisture. Use rat traps and keep cats if needed. For flour, it's perishable. Flour stays good for 3 months if kept dry and cool. But in humid areas like Mombasa, it can spoil in 6 weeks. So, produce to order. Don't overstock. Use a simple card system: each bag of wheat gets a tag with date and weight. When you use it, record it. For flour, stack bags on pallets, not directly on floor. Keep a minimum stock level: say, 2 days of wheat and 1 day of flour. That's your safety stock. Reorder when you hit that level. Use a notebook or a free app like 'Inventory Simple' on your phone. Count stock every Friday. Compare with records. If there's a difference, investigate. Maybe theft, spillage, or moisture loss. Also, rotate stock: first in, first out. Old wheat can get weevils. You can prevent weevils by adding diatomaceous earth (food grade) at 1 kg per tonne. For flour, sell older stock first. If you have a walk-in customer, sell the oldest bag. Finally, keep records for at least one year. This helps with loans and taxes.

lessons.title: Cost Analysis and Yield Optimization
lessons.body: To make a profit, you must know your costs. Let's break down a 50 kg bag of flour. First, wheat cost: In Kenya, wheat might be 40 KES per kg. But you don't use 50 kg of wheat to make 50 kg of flour. Extraction rate is key. For white flour, you get about 75% extraction. So, to get 50 kg flour, you need 66.7 kg wheat. That wheat costs 66.7 x 40 = 2,668 KES. Then milling costs: electricity, labor, maintenance, bags, and overhead. Suppose electricity is 500 KES per hour, and you mill 500 kg per hour. For 66.7 kg, that's 0.133 hours, so 66.7 KES. Labor: if you pay a worker 500 KES per day and they produce 70 bags, that's 7.14 KES per bag. Bags cost 30 KES each. Maintenance: set aside 2% of revenue, say 50 KES. Total cost: 2,668 + 66.7 + 7.14 + 30 + 50 = 2,821.84 KES. If you sell at 3,200 KES, profit is 378 KES per bag. But yield optimization can improve this. If you adjust the mill to get 78% extraction, you need only 64.1 kg wheat, saving 104 KES. Also, reduce downtime. If you mill 6 hours instead of 5, you spread fixed costs. Train staff to reduce waste. Spilled flour is money lost. A 1% spill on 50 kg is 0.5 kg, worth about 32 KES. So, sweep floors and use all flour. Also, consider by-products: bran sells for animal feed at 20 KES per kg. From 66.7 kg wheat, you get about 16.7 kg bran, worth 334 KES. That offsets costs. So, net cost becomes 2,821.84 - 334 = 2,487.84 KES. Profit now 712 KES per bag. Keep a daily cost sheet. Review weekly.

lessons.title: Staff Training and Supervision
lessons.body: Your staff are your most important asset. In a small mill, you might have 3-5 workers. They need training on safety, machinery, and quality. Start with safety: dust from flour can explode. So, no smoking, no open flames. Workers must wear masks and ear protection. Train them to lock out the mill before cleaning. In Nigeria, many accidents happen because someone turns on the mill while another is inside. So, use a padlock and key system. Only the supervisor has the key. For machinery, train on start-up and shut-down procedures. For a roller mill, start the rolls before feeding wheat. Shut down after all wheat is out. Teach them to listen for unusual noises. A bearing squeal means it needs grease. A knock means a loose bolt. Quality training: show how to check flour fineness. Rub a pinch between fingers. If it feels gritty, adjust the rolls. Also, teach moisture testing. A simple moisture meter costs about $100. If wheat is above 14% moisture, it can clog the mill. So, dry it first. Supervision: don't micromanage. Set clear daily targets: e.g., 70 bags. Check progress every 2 hours. Use a whiteboard to show targets and actual. Praise good work. If someone is slow, find out why. Maybe they need better tools. Rotate jobs so everyone can do every task. That way, if one person is absent, others cover. Hold a 15-minute meeting every Monday. Discuss last week's problems and solutions. Keep a training log: date, topic, who attended. This helps for audits. Finally, pay fairly and on time. A happy worker is a productive worker. In many African mills, high turnover is a problem. So, invest in your team.

lessons.title: Regulatory Compliance and Food Safety
lessons.body: Food safety is not optional. In most African countries, mills must register with the national food safety authority. For example, in Kenya, it's KEBS (Kenya Bureau of Standards). In Nigeria, NAFDAC. You need a license to sell flour. To get it, your mill must meet hygiene standards. Start with the building: walls should be smooth and washable. Floors should be concrete, not dirt. There should be no cracks where pests hide. Lighting must be bright enough to see dirt. Ventilation to remove dust. Water supply: clean water for cleaning. Handwashing stations with soap. Toilets must be separate from milling area. Pest control: use traps, not poison near flour. Keep a pest control log. Every week, check for rodent droppings. If found, clean and set traps. Personal hygiene: workers must wash hands before handling flour. Wear clean uniforms. No jewelry. Hairnets. If sick, stay home. For the product: flour must be free of foreign matter. Use magnets to catch metal bits. Sift flour before bagging. Also, label correctly. Include: product name, weight, ingredients, production date, expiry date, and your contact. For export, you need more: aflatoxin testing, moisture content, protein content. Keep records of every batch: wheat source, milling date, who milled it. If a customer complains, you can trace back. Also, train staff on allergens. If you mill different grains, clean between runs. Wheat is a common allergen. So, if you also mill maize, clean thoroughly. Finally, expect inspections. An inspector may come unannounced. Keep your records ready. If you fail, you get a warning or fine. So, do it right from the start.

lessons.title: Preventive Maintenance Programs
lessons.body: Preventive maintenance (PM) saves money. A breakdown costs 10 times more than a planned repair. Start with a schedule. For a small mill, you need daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly tasks. Daily: before start-up, check oil levels in the gearbox. Grease bearings. Check belt tension. Listen for unusual noises. After shutdown, clean the mill. Remove flour dust. Dust causes fires and clogs. Weekly: inspect rolls for wear. Use a micrometer to measure diameter. If worn more than 0.5 mm, regrind or replace. Check sifter screens for holes. A hole lets bran into white flour. Replace if torn. Monthly: change oil in the gearbox. Check electrical connections for loose wires. Tighten bolts on the mill frame. Vibration can loosen them. Clean the magnet. Test the emergency stop button. Yearly: overhaul the mill. Replace worn bearings. Check the main shaft for cracks. Repaint rusty areas. Also, maintain your generator. Change oil every 100 hours. Clean air filter every 50 hours. Keep spare parts: bearings, belts, screens, fuses. In Africa, getting parts can take weeks. So, stock critical spares. Keep a maintenance log: date, task, who did it, parts used. This helps predict failures. For example, if a bearing fails every 6 months, you know to replace it at 5 months. Train your staff to do daily checks. But for complex tasks, hire a technician. Budget for PM: set aside 3% of your revenue. For a mill making 1 million KES per month, that's 30,000 KES. Spend it on parts and labor. Don't skip PM. A mill that runs smoothly produces more flour and lasts longer.

quiz.q: What is the first step in production planning for a small mill?
quiz.explanation: Knowing capacity helps you plan how much wheat to buy and how many shifts to run.

quiz.q: Why should you schedule harder wheat first?
options: D) It is easier to mill
quiz.explanation: Harder wheat requires more power, so mill it when electricity is stable.

quiz.q: What is a good practice to reduce changeover time between flour types?
options: A) Mill all white flour first, then whole wheat
C) Clean the mill after every bag
D) Use the same settings for all flour
quiz.explanation: Grouping similar flour types reduces cleaning and adjustment time.

quiz.q: How often should you check for jams in the mill?
quiz.explanation: Hourly checks catch jams early, preventing long downtime.

quiz.q: What should be recorded in a daily production log?
options: A) Wheat used, flour produced, downtime
quiz.explanation: These data help identify inefficiencies and improve planning.

quiz.q: When is the best time to buy wheat in bulk in Tanzania?
quiz.explanation: Prices are lowest after harvest when supply is high.

quiz.q: Why should flour be stacked on pallets?
options: A) To prevent moisture from the floor
quiz.explanation: Pallets protect flour from dampness and pests.

quiz.q: What is a safety stock level?
options: A) Minimum inventory to cover delays
B) Maximum inventory you can store
D) Flour that is about to expire
quiz.explanation: Safety stock ensures you can keep milling if deliveries are late.

quiz.q: How can you prevent weevils in stored wheat?
quiz.explanation: Diatomaceous earth kills insects without chemicals.

quiz.q: What is the 'first in, first out' rule?
quiz.explanation: FIFO reduces spoilage and ensures quality.

quiz.q: If you need 50 kg of white flour and extraction rate is 75%, how much wheat do you need?
What is a by-product of milling wheat that can be sold?
quiz.explanation: Bran is used for animal feed and adds revenue.

quiz.q: How can you improve yield without buying new equipment?
options: A) Adjust mill to increase extraction rate
quiz.explanation: Proper adjustment can increase flour extracted from same wheat.

quiz.q: What is a fixed cost in milling?
quiz.explanation: Labor is often a fixed cost if workers are paid daily regardless of output.

quiz.q: Why is reducing spillage important?
quiz.explanation: Spilled flour is lost product and lost profit.

quiz.q: What should be included in a daily cost sheet?
quiz.explanation: These are the main variable costs per bag.

quiz.q: Why is dust explosion a risk in flour mills?
quiz.explanation: Fine flour dust can ignite and explode if confined.

quiz.q: What is a lockout/tagout procedure?
options: A) Locking the mill before maintenance
B) Locking the door at night
quiz.explanation: It prevents accidental start-up during maintenance.

quiz.q: How can you check flour fineness without a lab?
quiz.explanation: Grittiness indicates coarse flour; adjust rolls.

quiz.q: What is a good target for daily production?
quiz.explanation: Based on a 500 kg/hour mill running 7 hours, 70 bags is realistic.

quiz.q: Why should you rotate jobs among staff?
quiz.explanation: Cross-training ensures flexibility.

quiz.q: What should be discussed in a weekly staff meeting?
options: A) Last week's problems and solutions
quiz.explanation: Focus on continuous improvement.

quiz.q: Which organization regulates food safety in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: KEBS is the Kenya Bureau of Standards.

quiz.q: What is a requirement for mill building hygiene?
quiz.explanation: Smooth walls are easy to clean and discourage pests.

quiz.q: Why should you use magnets in the milling line?
quiz.explanation: Magnets remove metal contaminants that could damage equipment or harm consumers.

quiz.q: What must be on a flour label?
options: A) Production date and expiry date
quiz.explanation: Dates are critical for food safety and traceability.

quiz.q: What is preventive maintenance?
quiz.explanation: PM prevents unexpected breakdowns.

quiz.q: How often should you grease bearings in a small mill?
quiz.explanation: Daily greasing reduces wear and heat.

quiz.q: What should you check weekly in a roller mill?
quiz.explanation: Rolls wear out and affect flour quality.

quiz.q: Why keep a maintenance log?
quiz.explanation: Logs help identify recurring issues and plan replacements.
